A widget extension is a separate process with its own bundle identifier and a memory ceiling a fraction of the app's, so it shares your source code but never your app's running state.

### It is a different target, not the app
- Its bundle id must be prefixed by the app's, and it gets its own container, its own entitlements and its own Info.plist. Nothing your `AppDelegate` or `App.init` set up exists here — a singleton read in the widget is a fresh, empty instance of that singleton.
- Data crosses only through something both processes can open: an App Group container, the Keychain with an access group, or the network. There is no in-memory hand-off.
- The body is archived SwiftUI, so no `UIViewController`, no `UIView`, no timers and no animation loops. The only self-driving views are `Text(_:style:)`, `Text(timerInterval:)` and `ProgressView(timerInterval:)`.

### The ceiling
- Widget extensions are held to roughly 30 MB, and the system kills the process outright on breach — the slot shows an error plate instead of the widget. A full-size image decode is the usual killer: decode to the display size with `CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex`, or stage a downscaled copy in the group container.
- Each callback also gets only a few seconds; a slow timeline build is a killed extension, not a late widget.

The mental model: the extension is a rendering client for data the app has already prepared, not a second copy of the app.

The gallery calls `snapshot`, and it passes a context with `isPreview == true` — that call must return canned sample data immediately instead of waiting on a store or the network.

### The three callbacks
- `placeholder(in:)` — synchronous and instant. It is the skeleton WidgetKit renders redacted while the real view is being prepared, so hard-code sample values and do no I/O at all.
- `snapshot(for:in:)` — one entry for a single moment: the gallery, the widget's first appearance after it is placed, and transient system UI. Branch on `context.isPreview` and return a fixture; real data is fine here only when it is already local.
- `timeline(for:in:)` — an array of future entries plus a reload policy. This is the only callback that should touch a store or the network, and even it has a few seconds.

### What that means in practice
- `AppIntentTimelineProvider` (async, iOS 17+) replaced `IntentTimelineProvider` for configurable widgets; a `StaticConfiguration` widget still uses `TimelineProvider` with its completion-handler methods.
- An entry is just a `TimelineEntry`: a `date` at which it becomes the current entry, plus whatever your view needs.
- `context.family` tells you which size is being asked for, and `context.displaySize` its point size — the same provider serves every family.
- Signed-out is a normal state in the extension: render a useful logged-out entry rather than an empty view, because the gallery will show whatever you return.

Placeholder is a skeleton, snapshot is a poster, the timeline is the film.

A reload policy tells WidgetKit the earliest moment it may ask you for a new timeline — it is a request, not a schedule, and once the current timeline's entries are exhausted under `.never` nothing will ever ask again.

### The three policies
- `.atEnd` — ask for a new timeline after the last entry's date. A timeline of one entry dated now means "ask again immediately", which is how a widget spends its whole day's budget before lunch and then goes silent.
- `.after(date)` — ask no earlier than `date`. Use it when you know when the data can change: the next opening bell, midnight, the end of the shift.
- `.never` — the system will not ask on its own; only your app can wake it.

### Pushing the change from the app
- `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines(ofKind: "SalesWidget")` after a save, or `reloadAllTimelines()`. This only works while your app or one of its extensions is actually executing — an app that has not run since yesterday reloads nothing, which is the usual reason for a stale number.
- `currentConfigurations()` tells you which kinds the user has actually placed, so you do not spend reloads on widgets that do not exist.
- To move data while the app is dead you have to wake it: a background push handled in the app or a notification service extension, or a `BGAppRefreshTask`.

The durable fix is usually fewer reloads and more entries — if the data is predictable, return one timeline that already covers the rest of the day.

Each installed widget has a rolling daily budget of background reloads — Apple's guidance is roughly 40 to 70 a day, one every 15 to 60 minutes — and once it is spent the system quietly stops honouring your reload policy until it refills.

### What the budget counts
- The reloads the system performs for you: the ones your `.atEnd` or `.after` policy asked for, and the ones you requested with `WidgetCenter.reloadTimelines`.
- The size of the allowance is set by the user's behaviour, not yours: how often the widget is actually on screen, how often the app is used, whether the device is in Low Power Mode.
- Not counted: reloads while the containing app is in the foreground, and a reload caused by the user editing the widget's configuration. A tap on a `Button(intent:)` re-renders the widget as part of the interaction rather than out of the budget.
- A reload you win but cannot finish still counts — the extension has only a few seconds inside `timeline(for:in:)`.

### Lock Screen, StandBy and the escape hatch
- Lock Screen widgets are allowed a more generous allowance than Home Screen ones, because the Lock Screen is glanced at constantly; identical code and an identical policy simply update more often there. In StandBy at night and on an always-on display the system dims and slows updates instead.
- When the change is genuinely unpredictable, do not shorten the interval — send a background push that wakes the app, sync there, and reload the widget with data you already hold.

Budget it like network calls: every reload is a withdrawal, and entries you can compute forward are free.

In `AppIntentConfiguration` the choices come from an `EntityQuery` on an `AppEntity`, and that query runs inside the widget extension while the user edits the widget — never in your app.

### The pieces
- `AppIntentConfiguration(kind:intent:provider:)` takes a `WidgetConfigurationIntent`: a plain Swift struct with `@Parameter` properties. It replaced iOS 16's `IntentConfiguration`, its `.intentdefinition` file and the separate Intents extension that used to answer the options.
- A parameter whose values are dynamic is typed as an `AppEntity`. Its `EntityQuery` supplies `entities(for:)` to resolve identifiers the user picked earlier and `suggestedEntities()` for the list the picker shows. For plain values — a `String`, an enum — `DynamicOptionsProvider` is the lighter equivalent.
- The provider becomes an `AppIntentTimelineProvider`, and every callback is handed the configured intent instance, so `timeline(for configuration:in:)` reads `configuration.project` directly.

### The traps
- The query executes with the extension's memory, the extension's few seconds, and possibly before the app has ever been launched. Read the App Group container or a cached list; a cold API call there is what leaves the configuration sheet spinning.
- `entities(for:)` must survive an identifier that no longer exists — return an empty array and give the timeline a sensible default, rather than throwing and sending the widget to the error plate.
- Migrating a shipped iOS 16 widget: Xcode's intent-definition editor has a Convert to App Intent action. Keep the generated type and parameter names exactly as it produced them, or every widget already on a Home Screen loses its configuration.

A widget is interactive only through `Button(intent:)` and `Toggle(isOn:intent:)`, the tap runs an `AppIntent` outside the render pass, and it is `.invalidatableContent()` that makes the wait look deliberate instead of broken.

### What is allowed
- Those two controls, and only their `intent:` initialisers. `onTapGesture`, a `NavigationLink`, a `TextField`, a drag — all inert in a widget; the tap falls through to the widget's `widgetURL` and launches the app instead.
- The intent is performed in the background, with your app woken if it is not running. It gets a few seconds, so a real upload belongs in a background `URLSession`, not inside `perform()`.
- `perform()` must write where the widget can read it back — the App Group store — because a widget view holds no state of its own; it is re-rendered from a timeline entry every time.

### Making the tap feel instant
- `.invalidatableContent()` marks the parts of the view the tap makes stale. The system renders them in a pending style the moment the intent starts, so the row reacts before the work is done.
- `Toggle(isOn:intent:)` flips optimistically by itself and reverts only if `perform()` throws — swallow the error and you have drawn a lie.
- When the intent returns, WidgetKit reloads that widget for you. Call `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines(ofKind:)` yourself only for the *other* widget kinds your change also affects.
- If the action genuinely needs UI, conform to `OpenIntent` or set `openAppWhenRun = true` — that is a foreground launch, so it is the exception, not the pattern.

`Link` gives per-element destinations but only in the medium, large and extra-large families; everywhere else — small widgets and every Lock Screen accessory family — the whole widget is a single tap target and only `.widgetURL` applies.

### The two APIs
- `.widgetURL(_:)` sets one destination for the entire widget. Apply exactly one: several `widgetURL` modifiers in the same tree give undefined behaviour, and a row view quietly carrying its own is the usual reason every row opens the same screen.
- `Link(destination:)` gives each row its own URL and is ignored outside `systemMedium`, `systemLarge` and `systemExtraLarge`. Use both together — a `Link` per row, and `widgetURL` at the root as the fallback for taps that land in the padding.
- A `Button(intent:)` is not a link: it runs its intent instead of opening anything, and its area no longer belongs to the surrounding `Link`.

### Handling the open
- The app receives the URL through `onOpenURL` in SwiftUI, or `scene(_:openURLContexts:)` in UIKit. It is a cold launch as often as not, so the handler has to build the destination from the URL alone.
- Encode a stable identifier, never an array index or an in-memory object — the entry that rendered the view may be hours old and the list behind it has moved on.
- A custom scheme is enough; a universal link is the same code and also works from the web and from Messages.

Check the small family and one Lock Screen family before shipping: that is exactly where a `Link`-based design quietly stops working.

Everything that can change during the activity goes in `ContentState`; everything else goes in the attributes, which are fixed at `request` time and can never be updated afterwards.

### The split
- `ActivityAttributes` is the static half — order id, restaurant name, an image name that ships in the extension's bundle. It is handed to the widget extension once when the activity starts and is immutable for its whole life.
- The nested `ContentState`, which must be `Codable & Hashable`, is the dynamic half: step, ETA, courier name if it can still change. Each update replaces it wholesale, and the system diffs the new value against the old to animate — an identical state produces no visible change at all.
- Get it wrong and there is no live fix: correcting a value that lives in the attributes means ending this activity and requesting a new one, which the user sees as the card disappearing and a different one appearing.

### Size and lifecycle
- The dynamic payload is capped at 4 KB. Put identifiers in the state and let the view read the detail from the App Group container; images must already exist in the extension's bundle or that container, because nothing downloads from a Live Activity's view.
- `Activity.request(attributes:content:pushType:)` works only from the foreground — unless the server starts it with a push-to-start token — and only when `ActivityAuthorizationInfo().areActivitiesEnabled` is true.
- `ActivityContent(state:staleDate:relevanceScore:)` carries more than the state: past `staleDate` the view can read `context.isStale` and admit it may be out of date, and `relevanceScore` orders your own competing activities.
- After a relaunch your `Activity` handle is gone — recover it from `Activity<DeliveryAttributes>.activities` instead of starting a second one.

Two different tokens: a push-to-start token that belongs to the activity *type* and exists before anything is running, and a per-activity token you only get after that particular activity has started.

### The two tokens
- `Activity<DeliveryAttributes>.pushToStartTokenUpdates` is an `AsyncSequence` you subscribe to at launch. It requires `NSSupportsLiveActivities` in the app's Info.plist, and it hands the server a token that can start an activity when none is running.
- `activity.pushTokenUpdates` is the per-activity token. It arrives *after* `Activity.request(..., pushType: .token)` returns and it can rotate, so registering only the first value you see is the classic reason updates stop landing halfway through a delivery.

### The APNs request
- Headers are `apns-push-type: liveactivity` and `apns-topic: <bundle-id>.push-type.liveactivity`.
- The `aps` dictionary carries `timestamp`, `event` (`start`, `update` or `end`) and `content-state`; a start push also needs `attributes-type` and `attributes`. `stale-date` tells the UI when to show its stale style, `dismissal-date` on an end push controls how long the finished activity lingers.
- The payload cap is 4 KB — put an id in the state and let the widget read the rest from the App Group.

### The clock
- The system force-ends an activity 8 hours after it starts, and removes it from the Lock Screen 12 hours after that start. The per-activity token dies with it; the push-to-start token survives, so a longer job means starting a fresh activity, not reviving the old one.
- Rapid updates need `NSSupportsLiveActivitiesFrequentUpdates` plus a check of `ActivityAuthorizationInfo().frequentPushesEnabled` — the user can switch it off.

The compact presentation is only used when yours is the *only* active Live Activity; as soon as a second app has one, the system falls back to the minimal presentation for both.

### The four presentations
- `compactLeading` and `compactTrailing` are the two slivers either side of the sensor housing. One app at a time gets them.
- `minimal` is a single circle-sized view. With two activities the system shows one minimal attached to the Island and the other detached to its right; with more, it picks by recency and `relevanceScore`, which you cannot override.
- The expanded layout is assembled from `DynamicIslandExpandedRegion(.leading)`, `.trailing`, `.center` and `.bottom`, and appears on long press. Keep it under roughly 160 points tall — past that the system truncates it.
- The Lock Screen view in `ActivityConfiguration` is not optional. Devices without an Island use it, and it is also what appears as a banner when an update arrives.

### What catches people
- A `minimal` view that is only a progress ring is unidentifiable once it is detached from your app's context. Put a glyph in it.
- The compact views are tiny — a `Text` with a `.timer` style needs a fixed `frame(width:)` or it will wobble as digits change width.
- Taps do not expand anything: `.widgetURL` on the `DynamicIsland` handles compact and minimal, and `Link` works inside expanded regions. Without either, a tap opens the app at its last screen.
- `.keylineTint()` colours the ring the system draws around the compact and minimal presentations — it is the only branding you get at that size.

Design the minimal view first: it is the presentation you are most likely to actually get.

A widget is rendered in three modes — `.fullColor`, `.accented` and `.vibrant` — and the last two discard your colours, so anything that carries meaning in hue alone stops carrying it.

### containerBackground
- Since iOS 17 the background must be declared with `.containerBackground(for: .widget) { … }`. A widget that paints its own with `.background(…)` renders on a blank plate in StandBy, on the iPad Lock Screen and in the tinted Home Screen appearance, because the system removes the container background in exactly those contexts and yours is not the container background.
- `.containerBackgroundRemovable(false)` declares that the background *is* the content — a photo widget. The price is that the widget is no longer offered in StandBy or on the iPad Lock Screen.

### The rendering modes
- Read the mode from `@Environment(\.widgetRenderingMode)`.
- `.fullColor` — Home Screen in the standard appearance, and StandBy in daylight.
- `.vibrant` — Lock Screen widgets and StandBy at night. Content is desaturated and mapped onto a monochrome material *by luminance*, so pale grey on white simply vanishes.
- `.accented` — tinted Home Screen icons and watchOS. The system splits the view tree into two groups: what you marked `.widgetAccentable(true)` gets the user's accent colour, everything else is desaturated. `.widgetAccentedRenderingMode(_:)` decides how an individual `Image` is treated.

### The rule
Never encode state in colour alone — pair it with a glyph or a word — and preview each mode with `.environment(\.widgetRenderingMode, .accented)` before you ship. `AccessoryWidgetBackground()` gives Lock Screen accessory widgets the standard translucent plate rather than one you invent.

`completeRequest` tears the extension process down at once, and the system kills it anyway when the sheet dismisses, so any in-process transfer dies with it — the extension's job is to hand the file off, not to send it.

### Getting the file out of the item
- `extensionContext!.inputItems` is an array of `NSExtensionItem`; the payload lives in each item's `attachments`, an array of `NSItemProvider`.
- Use `loadFileRepresentation(for: .movie)`. It gives you a URL that is **deleted when the closure returns**, so copy or move the file before you leave it. `loadDataRepresentation` reads the whole thing into memory and jetsams the extension long before 200 MB — an extension gets a fraction of the app's memory allowance, not the app's.
- Copy it into the App Group container: that is the only directory the containing app can also open.

### Handing the upload off
- Enqueue a `URLSession` background session created with `URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier:)`, and set `sharedContainerIdentifier` to the App Group. That property is mandatory inside an extension; without it the transfer never starts.
- Background sessions accept only file-backed bodies, so it is `uploadTask(with:fromFile:)` — an `httpBody` is silently ignored.
- Once the extension is gone the system relaunches the *containing app* in the background and calls `application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:)`. That is where progress, retries and the success toast belong.

`NSExtensionActivationRule` in the extension's Info.plist decides whether your app is even offered for that item type — a rule that matches everything is why testers see you in the share sheet for a PDF you cannot handle.

An `AppIntent` on its own only reaches the Shortcuts app; to be voice- and Spotlight-invocable out of the box it must also be declared in an `AppShortcutsProvider`, with phrases that name the app and a `parameterSummary` that reads as a sentence.

### What each piece buys you
- `AppIntent` — `title`, `description`, `@Parameter` properties and `perform() async throws -> some IntentResult`. That is enough to appear as a building block in Shortcuts, and nothing more.
- `AppShortcutsProvider.appShortcuts` — up to **10** `AppShortcut`s per app, registered when the app is installed. These are what Siri recognises and what Spotlight surfaces without the user ever opening Shortcuts.
- Every phrase must interpolate `\(.applicationName)`; the build fails without it, because that token is how Siri disambiguates your app from every other one. Give several natural wordings, plus `shortTitle` and `systemImageName` for the tile.

### parameterSummary
- `Summary("Log a \(\.$size) \(\.$drink)")` is the sentence shown in the Shortcuts editor and read back by Siri. Parameters left out of it are collapsed behind "Show More", so a required parameter you forgot to mention looks to the user like it has no value at all.
- Use `When(\.$kind, .equalTo, .custom) { Summary(…) } otherwise: { Summary(…) }` when a parameter only matters in one branch.
- A parameter Siri has to ask for needs `@Parameter(title:requestValueDialog:)`, otherwise the prompt is a generic "What value?".

### Parameters that are your model objects
Make the type an `AppEntity` with a `DisplayRepresentation` and an `EntityQuery`; use `EntityStringQuery` so a spoken word can be resolved to a record. Call `MyShortcuts.updateAppShortcutParameters()` after the underlying list changes, and conform the entity to `IndexedEntity` to donate it to Spotlight's index.

You get roughly 30 seconds, and if you have not called the content handler by then the system delivers the *original* payload — a slow attachment download is exactly how a rich push degrades back into plain text.

### The contract
- `UNNotificationServiceExtension` runs only for pushes sent with `mutable-content: 1` and an `alert` payload. A `content-available` silent push never reaches it.
- `didReceive(_:withContentHandler:)` hands you the request; you mutate a copy of `request.content` and call the handler exactly once.
- Keep the handler *and* your best-effort content in properties, because `serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire()` is your last chance to call it. Do the cheap, must-have work — decrypting the body — first, so the timeout costs you the picture and not the message.

### Downloading the attachment
- Download to disk with `downloadTask`, then build `UNNotificationAttachment(identifier:url:options:)`. The system **moves** that file into its own store, and `URLSession`'s temporary URL is deleted when the completion handler returns, so move it somewhere you own first.
- The file needs a real path extension or an explicit `UNNotificationAttachmentOptionsTypeHintKey`; a mismatched type is silently dropped. Limits are 10 MB for images, 5 MB audio, 50 MB video.
- Set `timeoutIntervalForRequest` to 10–15 seconds, well inside the budget, and never load the body into memory — the extension's ceiling is a couple of dozen megabytes.

The mental model is best-effort decoration: the notification has to read correctly with zero modification, and everything the extension adds is a bonus it may not get. A small, CDN-cached thumbnail URL on the server side buys more reliability than any code in here.

The widget runs in a separate, system-launched process that Xcode is not attached to when you run the app scheme, so you attach to the extension deliberately and log through `Logger` instead of `print`.

### Getting a debugger onto it
- Select the *widget extension* scheme and Run. Xcode installs the containing app, waits for the extension to be launched by the system, and attaches to it; pick the containing app when asked what to run.
- Or run the app normally, then `Debug > Attach to Process by PID or Name`, type the extension's executable name, and force a launch by calling `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadAllTimelines()` from the app.
- `#Preview(as: .systemSmall) { … } timeline: { … }` is the fast loop, but it renders inside the *app's* process. It will never reproduce a missing App Group entitlement or a memory kill.

### Where the output went
- `print` writes to stdout, and nobody is capturing stdout for a process the system launched. Use `Logger(subsystem:category:)`: it shows in Console.app, in `xcrun simctl spawn booted log stream --predicate 'subsystem == "…"'`, and in Xcode once attached.
- Interpolated values are redacted to `<private>` unless you pass `privacy: .public`.

### What "Unable to Load" actually means
- The extension crashed or was jetsammed, and by far the most common cause is the widget's memory ceiling — a fraction of the app's. Decode images to the size you draw them at; a full-resolution asset is a reliable `EXC_RESOURCE (RESOURCE_TYPE_MEMORY)`.
- The crash report is filed against the extension's executable, not the app: on device under Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements > Analytics Data, or Xcode's Devices and Simulators > View Device Logs; from TestFlight and the App Store, Organizer > Crashes.
- A provider that returns without calling its completion handler looks identical to a crash — check every path, including the error one.

A control's displayed value comes from a `ControlValueProvider` running in the widget extension on the system's schedule, never from your app, so a state change made anywhere else has to be published to shared storage and followed by `ControlCenter.shared.reloadControls(ofKind:)`.

### What a control is
- A `ControlWidget` lives in the same widget extension as your widgets. Its body is a `ControlWidgetConfiguration` wrapping exactly one `ControlWidgetButton` or `ControlWidgetToggle`, and that single declaration serves Control Centre, the Lock Screen slots and the Action button.
- The action is an `AppIntent`: a `SetValueIntent` for a toggle, a plain `AppIntent` for a button. It runs in the background without launching the app, so it has to do its work over the network or through shared state. If it truly needs the UI, conform to `OpenIntent` or set `openAppWhenRun = true`; camera-style controls use `CameraCaptureIntent`.

### Keeping the value honest
- `StaticControlConfiguration` takes a `ControlValueProvider` with a `previewValue` — used in the gallery, so it must not do I/O — and an async `currentValue()`. That runs inside the extension, so it reads the App Group container or the network; it cannot ask the running app.
- The system refreshes it on its own budget, the same way it refreshes timelines. Every state change the control did not cause itself — the app, a push, another device — must end with `ControlCenter.shared.reloadControls(ofKind:)`.
- A toggle flips optimistically the instant it is tapped and reverts only if the intent **throws**. Swallow the error and you have painted a lock that never locked.

All of this happens while the device may be locked, so whatever the provider reads must be available after first unlock rather than only while unlocked.
